newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FEATURE - Troubleshooting Swiss diplomat keeps low profile.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Troubleshooting Swiss diplomat keeps low profile.

text.p: Thomas Borer is quite happpy to defend Switzerland against accusations that it collaborated with the Nazis and that its banks hoarded the unclaimed wealth of Holocaust victims, but he doesn't like talking about himself.
In an interview before leaving for the U.S. to meet some of Switzerland's most vocal critics, the ambassador talked in a somewhat reticent Swiss fashion about his ambitions and his worries.

Does he have special role models -- Churchill or Metternich perhaps? "No. That would be too big. I wanted to be just a good, modest Swiss diplomat," replied 39-year-old Borer, who aspired to a diplomatic career from the age of 12.
Borer, who has a law degree, worked in the private sector before joining the diplomatic corps. He once served in Washington as legal counsel to the Swiss embassy.

He stepped into the limelight in October when he took on leadership of the task force coordinating the Swiss response to criticism that it may have profited from its neutral status by dealing with the Nazis.
Quoted in the media, interviewed on television, he is as close as one gets in Switzerland to a political personality. This makes him uncomfortable.
"I don't like these soft features," he said. "Especially other people do not like that."
One Swiss tabloid even did a feature about Borer's American girlfriend. She lives in Dallas.
"Yes, of course you can mention that I have an American girlfriend," said Borer, requesting her name not be used.
How did they meet?
"At a ball. She was very impressed that I know who Buddy Holly is. Every Swiss knows Buddy Holly."
What Borer will not say publicly, but others in the country say privately, is that being in the public eye is not quite proper here. It invites criticism, even jealousy.
But it is hard to stay out of view when you are coordinating efforts to respond to what has been a public relations disaster.
The discussions have not only pitted Swiss against the rest of the world, but against each other. On television, Borer has deplored the Swiss tendency to "shoot each other in the knee."
"We criticise each other very much. We do not really support each other," he said.
Borer declined to give specific examples of this at a time when prominent names have been cast uncomfortably into the spotlight.

Economics Minister Jean-Pascal Delamuraz, in an interview at the end of his year as Swiss president, compared calls to set up a Holocaust victims' memorial fund to "blackmail." He later apologised amid international uproar.

A short time later, one of the country's biggest banks, Union Bank of Switzerland, owned up to what it termed an "unfortunate mistake" when it shredded some historic documents pertaining to a bank it acquired in 1945.
TASK TO REPAIR PUBLIC RELATIONS DISASTER
Borer's job, which takes 16 hours a day, seven days a week, is to somehow set right such public relations disasters and to act as a liaison.

He spoke before the U.S. House of Representatives Banking Committee in December, a moment he calls his "greatest personal success. There, for the first time, I could raise a Swiss voice and people believed me," he said.

While defending Swiss interests, along with a staff of 20, he is helping to dredge up the dispassionate truth, as much as is possible, about an era in which six million Jews, along with innumerable other victims, were slaughtered.
Need an 80-page document, in English, on the issue of assets belonging to Jews in Hungary and Poland? Borer has it.
He calls U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato, chairman of the Senate Banking Committee and a leading critic of Swiss banks' handling of Holocaust victims' assets, "very charming."

"Unfortunately, in Switzerland, he (D'Amato) is perceived as an adversary, but I would not perceive him as an adversary. I found myself establishing quite a good working relationship with him," Borer said.
D'Amato's role has been a mixed blessing for Switzerland, which Borer says would not have looked so thoroughly into its past without pressure from the outside.
But, he says even in this respect, patience is needed.

"You know, I think a lot of people accuse us of dragging our feet. But if you look and compare this political issue with other political issues, we are not only on a fast track, we are on a speed track," Borer said.
"We needed certainly a little bit of pressure, but on the other hand, did we need so much pressure? I don't think it was positive and constructive."
